paragraphs: PROLOGUE.
From about two hundred and thirty cases, all resembling to some degree the one I have called “Green Tea,” I have selected the following. I call it “The Familiar.”

As was his custom, Doctor Hesselius attached some sheets of writing paper to this manuscript. They contain his own observations on the case, written in handwriting almost as compact as print. He writes—

“For honesty and conscientiousness, no narrator could be more trustworthy than the venerable Irish clergyman who gave me this account of Mr. Barton’s case. Medically, however, the statement is incomplete. An intelligent physician who had followed the illness and attended the patient from its early stages to the end could have supplied the missing information. That would have enabled me to give a confident opinion. I would have known Mr. Barton’s likely hereditary tendencies. Very early symptoms might also have revealed something about an earlier origin of the disease than we can now establish.

“Broadly speaking, we can divide all similar cases into three distinct classes, based on the fundamental distinction between subjective and objective experience. Some people whose senses are said to receive supernatural impressions are simply seeing visions. The illusions they complain of originate in their own diseased brains or nerves. Others are unquestionably plagued by what we call spiritual forces existing outside themselves. Still others suffer from a combination of the two conditions. Their inner sense has indeed been opened, but disease has opened it and continues to keep it open. In one respect, this disease can be compared to losing the outer layer of skin. This exposes surfaces so sensitive that nature has provided them with a protective covering. Without that covering, they remain vulnerable to influences from which they were meant to be protected. In the brain, however, and in the nerves directly connected with its functions and sensory impressions, the circulation periodically undergoes a vibratory disturbance. I believe I have satisfactorily examined and demonstrated this in my manuscript essay, A. 17. As I prove there, this vibratory disturbance differs fundamentally from the congestive disturbance whose effects are examined in A. 19. When excessive, it is invariably accompanied by illusions.

“If I had seen Mr. Barton and examined him on the points in his case that need clarification, I could easily have traced these phenomena to the disease responsible for them. As it is, my diagnosis must remain a matter of conjecture.”
So writes Doctor Hesselius. He adds a great deal more that would interest only a physician trained in science.
The following chapters contain the account of the Rev. Thomas Herbert, which supplies everything known about the case.
CHAPTER I.
FOOT-STEPS.

I was a young man then, and knew some of the people involved in this strange story intimately. Its events therefore left a deep and lasting impression on me. I will now try to relate them all accurately. In doing so, I will bring together whatever I have learned from different sources that may shed even a little light on the darkness surrounding the course of the story and its ending.

Around the year 1794, the younger brother of a baronet whom I shall call Sir James Barton returned to Dublin. He had served with some distinction in the navy, commanding one of His Majesty’s frigates through most of the American war. Captain Barton appeared to be about forty-two or forty-three. He was an intelligent and pleasant companion when he chose, although generally reserved and sometimes even moody.

In company, however, he behaved like an experienced man of the world and a gentleman. He had acquired none of the loud, rough manners sometimes picked up at sea. On the contrary, his manner was remarkably relaxed, quiet and even polished. He was of medium height and rather strongly built. Thought had left lines on his face, which generally wore a serious and melancholy expression. As I have said, he was impeccably well-mannered, came from a good family and was wealthy. Naturally, those qualifications alone gave him ready admission to the best society in Dublin.

Mr. Barton’s personal habits were inexpensive. He rented rooms in one of the streets then fashionable on the south side of the city, and kept only one horse and one servant. Although reputed to be a freethinker, he lived an orderly and moral life. He indulged in neither gambling nor drinking, nor any other vicious pursuit. He kept largely to himself, formed no close friendships and chose no regular companions. He seemed to join fashionable society for its bustle and distraction, rather than for any chance to exchange thoughts or feelings with the people devoted to it.

Barton was therefore considered a thrifty, prudent, unsociable sort of fellow. He seemed likely to remain a bachelor in the face of every scheme and direct attack, live to a good old age, die rich and leave his money to a hospital.

It now became clear, however, that Mr. Barton’s intentions had been completely misunderstood. A young lady whom I shall call Miss Montague was being introduced to fashionable society by her aunt, the Dowager Lady L——. Miss Montague was decidedly pretty and accomplished. With some natural intelligence and a very lively manner, she became, for a time, one of society’s reigning favourites.

For a while, however, her popularity brought her nothing beyond insubstantial admiration. Such admiration may be a pleasing incense to vanity, but it does not necessarily lead to marriage. Unfortunately for Miss Montague, everyone understood that, apart from her personal attractions, she had no financial resources whatever. It is easy to imagine, then, the considerable surprise when Captain Barton appeared as the openly declared admirer of the penniless Miss Montague.

His courtship prospered, as might have been expected. Before long, old Lady L—— told each of her hundred and fifty particular friends, one after another, that Captain Barton had actually proposed to her niece, Miss Montague, with her approval. Her niece had accepted his hand, subject to her father’s consent. He was then sailing home from India and was expected within two or three weeks at the latest.

There could be no doubt that her father would consent, so the delay was only a formality. The pair were regarded as firmly engaged. With a strictness of old-fashioned propriety that her niece would doubtless have gladly done without, Lady L—— now withdrew her from all further participation in the city’s social festivities.

Captain Barton visited constantly and was frequently entertained at the house. He was allowed all the familiar privileges usually granted to a fiancé. This was how matters stood when the mysterious circumstances that darken this story first began to unfold.

Lady L—— lived in a handsome mansion on the north side of Dublin. Captain Barton’s lodgings, as already mentioned, were on the south. The distance between them was considerable. Whenever he spent the evening with the old lady and the beautiful young woman in her care, he generally walked home without a servant.
The shortest route on these nighttime walks took him for a considerable distance along a street that had so far only been laid out. Little more than the foundations of the houses had been built.

One night, shortly after becoming engaged to Miss Montague, he stayed unusually late with her and Lady L——. They had been discussing the evidence for divine revelation, which he disputed with the cold scepticism of a confirmed unbeliever. In those days, what were called “French principles” had spread widely through fashionable society, especially among those who supported the Whigs. Neither the old lady nor her niece was sufficiently free of that taint to regard Mr. Barton’s views as a serious objection to the proposed marriage.

The discussion had degenerated into talk about the supernatural and the marvellous, and he pursued exactly the same course of argument and ridicule. It must be said that Captain Barton was not putting on an act. The doctrines he insisted on really were, only too truly, the foundations of his settled belief, if belief it could be called. Perhaps one of the strangest facts in this strange story concerns the very man who suffered the fearful influences I am about to describe. For years, from a conviction he had deliberately reached, he had been a complete disbeliever in what are usually called supernatural agencies.

It was well past midnight when Mr. Barton said goodbye and set out alone for home. He reached the lonely road, where unfinished low walls on either side marked the foundations of the planned row of houses. The moon shone through mist, its uncertain light making the road even more desolate. An absolute silence lay over the place, carrying that indefinable sense of excitement such silence can create. Only his footsteps broke it, sounding unnaturally loud and distinct.
He had gone some distance when he suddenly heard other footsteps pattering at a steady pace, seemingly about forty steps behind him.

The suspicion that someone is following us is always unpleasant, and especially so in such a lonely place. It grew so strong in Captain Barton’s mind that he abruptly turned to face his pursuer. But there was enough moonlight to reveal anything on the road he had just walked, and no figure of any kind was visible.

The steps could not have been an echo of his own. He stamped his foot and walked briskly back and forth, trying in vain to produce one. Although he was not someone given to fanciful ideas, he finally had to put the sounds down to his imagination and dismiss them as an illusion. Satisfied with that explanation, he continued on his way. Before he had gone a dozen paces, the mysterious footsteps sounded behind him again. This time they seemed determined to prove they were not an echo. They sometimes slowed almost to a halt, sometimes broke into a run for six or eight strides, and then slowed to a walk again.

Captain Barton turned suddenly, as before, with the same result. Nothing was visible above the deserted surface of the road. He walked back over the same ground, determined to discover whatever had caused these unsettling sounds. His search, however, found nothing.

Despite all his scepticism, he felt something like superstitious fear rapidly creeping over him. With these unfamiliar and uncomfortable feelings, he turned once more and continued on his way. The haunting sounds did not return until he reached the place where he had last stopped and turned back. There they began again, with sudden bursts of running that threatened to bring the unseen pursuer right up to the frightened walker.

Captain Barton stopped again. The inexplicable nature of what was happening filled him with vague, unpleasant feelings. Giving way to his growing agitation, he called out sternly, “Who goes there?” There is something deeply unsettling about hearing one’s own voice raised in complete solitude, followed by total silence. Perhaps nothing in his life had ever made him so nervous.

The footsteps followed him to the very end of that lonely street. Only a strong effort of stubborn pride kept him from giving in to the urge, which returned every moment, to run for safety as fast as he could. Not until he reached his lodgings and sat beside his own fire did he feel calm enough to put the disturbing events in order and reconsider them. So little, after all, is needed to overthrow the pride of scepticism and prove the force of the old, simple laws of human nature within us.
CHAPTER II.
THE WATCHER.

The next morning, Mr. Barton sat over a late breakfast, reflecting on the previous night with more curiosity than fear. So quickly do gloomy impressions fade from the imagination in the cheerful light of day. While he sat there, a letter just delivered by the postman was placed on the table before him.

There was nothing unusual about the address except the unfamiliar handwriting. Perhaps it was disguised, for its tall, narrow letters leaned backwards. With the suspense people so often impose on themselves in such circumstances, he puzzled over the address for a full minute before breaking the seal. Inside, he read the following words, written in the same hand—

“Mr. Barton, formerly captain of the ‘Dolphin,’ is warned of DANGER. He would be wise to avoid —— street—[here the place of his adventure the previous night was named]. If he walks there as usual, he will meet with misfortune. Let him take this warning once and for all, for he has reason to dread
“THE WATCHER.”

Captain Barton read and reread this strange message. He turned it over and over, examining it in every light and from every direction. He studied the paper and inspected the handwriting again. Finding nothing there, he turned to the seal. It was only a patch of wax, with the faint, accidental impression of a thumb.

There was not the smallest mark or clue to suggest even a guess at where it had come from. The writer seemed to mean him well, yet signed himself as someone he had “reason to dread.” The letter, its author and its real purpose were an inexplicable puzzle. Worse, it unpleasantly brought to mind other associations connected with his adventure the previous night.

Some feeling, perhaps pride, kept Mr. Barton from telling even his intended bride about the events I have just described. Trivial as they might seem, they had deeply and unpleasantly affected his imagination. He did not want to disclose anything that even she might regard as evidence of weakness. The letter could easily have been a hoax, and the mysterious footsteps a delusion or a trick. Although he pretended the whole affair was not worth a thought, it continued to haunt him. Puzzling doubts tormented him, and fears he could not define weighed him down. What is certain is that for a considerable time afterwards, he carefully avoided the street named in the letter as the place of danger.

About a week passed after he received the letter I have copied before anything further reminded Captain Barton of its contents. Until then, the unpleasant impressions it had left were gradually fading from his mind.

One night, after that interval, he was returning from the theatre, which was then in Crow-street. He had seen Miss Montague and Lady L—— into their carriage, and lingered for a while with two or three acquaintances.

He parted from them near the college and continued alone. It was already one o’clock, and the streets were completely deserted. Throughout his walk with the companions he had just left, he had been painfully aware, at intervals, of footsteps that seemed to be following them.

Once or twice he had looked back, uneasy at the thought that the mysterious disturbance of a week earlier was about to begin again. He desperately hoped to see someone whose presence would explain the sounds naturally. But the street was deserted. No one was visible.
Now that he was walking home entirely alone, he grew truly nervous and uncomfortable. The familiar sounds, which he had come to dread absolutely, were becoming more distinct.

Along the blank wall surrounding the college park, the sounds followed him, starting again almost at the same instant as his own steps. Behind him came the same uneven pace: sometimes slow, sometimes quickening almost to a run for twenty yards or so. Again and again he turned. Almost every half-dozen steps, he darted a quick, secretive glance over his shoulder. No one was visible.

The distress caused by this unseen, elusive pursuit gradually became almost unbearable. By the time he reached home, his nerves were so agitated that he could not rest. He did not even try to lie down until after dawn.

A knock at his bedroom door woke him. His servant came in and handed him several letters just received by the one-penny post. One immediately caught his attention. A single glance at the address made him fully alert. He recognised the handwriting at once and read—

“Captain Barton, you might as well think you can escape your own shadow as escape me. Whatever you do, I will see you as often as I please, and you will see me. I do not want to hide myself, as you imagine. Do not let it disturb your rest, Captain Barton. With a clear conscience, why should you fear the eye of
“THE WATCHER.”

There is hardly any need to describe the feelings with which he read this strange message. For several days afterwards, people noticed that Captain Barton was unusually distracted and low in spirits, but no one guessed why.

Whatever he might think of the phantom footsteps that followed him, there could be no illusion about the letters he had received. Their arrival immediately after the mysterious sounds that had haunted him was, to say the least, an odd coincidence.
In his mind, the whole affair was vaguely and instinctively connected with certain episodes in his past—the very ones he most hated to remember.

Fortunately for him, perhaps, Captain Barton had something besides his approaching marriage to occupy him just then. He was deeply involved in settling a large claim on certain properties, a claim that had long been fought over in court.

The rush and excitement of business had their natural effect. They gradually dispelled the gloom that had occasionally weighed on him for a time. Before long, his spirits had completely returned to their usual level.

Throughout this period, however, he was still sometimes disturbed by faint, half-heard repetitions of the same sounds. They came in lonely places, by daylight as well as after dark. These returns of the strange sensations that had distressed him so much were scattered and indistinct. Often he could not tell, even to his own satisfaction, whether he had really heard them or merely imagined them in his agitated state.

One evening he walked to the House of Commons with a Member who was an acquaintance of both his and mine. I was with them; it was one of the few occasions on which I was in Captain Barton’s company. As we walked, I noticed him becoming so distracted and silent that he seemed to be weighed down by some urgent, consuming anxiety.
I later learned that throughout our walk, he had heard the familiar footsteps following him as we went.
This, however, was the last time he suffered that particular form of the persecution that was already causing him such anxiety. A new and very different form was about to appear.
CHAPTER III.
AN ADVERTISEMENT.
That evening, I witnessed the first of the new experiences that would gradually bring about his fate. Without its connection to the events that followed, I would scarcely remember the incident now.

As we entered the passage from College-Green, a man came very quickly straight towards us, apparently in a state of fierce agitation. He was muttering rapidly and vehemently to himself. All I remember of his appearance is that he was short, looked like a foreigner and wore a kind of fur travelling-cap.

This odd-looking person walked straight up to Barton, who was ahead of the other two of us. He stopped and stared at him for a moment or two with an expression of mad menace and fury. Then, just as abruptly, he turned, walked ahead of us at the same agitated pace and disappeared into a side passage. I distinctly remember being considerably shocked by the man’s face and manner. They forced on me a vague sense of danger unlike anything I have ever felt, before or since, in the presence of a human being. Yet those feelings were nowhere near strong enough to leave me flustered or agitated. I had seen only a remarkably evil face, stirred, as it seemed, by the excitement of madness.

The effect of this appearance on Captain Barton, however, absolutely astonished me. I knew him to be proudly courageous and calm in real danger, which made his behaviour all the stranger. As the man approached, Barton stepped back a pace or two and clutched my arm without a word. He seemed seized by a spasm of agony or terror! Then, as the figure disappeared, he shoved me roughly back and followed it for a few paces. He stopped in great agitation and sat down on a bench. I have never seen a face so ghastly and haggard.
“For God’s sake, Barton, what’s wrong?” asked ——, our companion, genuinely alarmed by his appearance. “You aren’t hurt, are you? Or ill? What is it?”
“What did he say? I didn’t hear it—what was it?” Barton asked, completely ignoring the question.
“Nonsense,” said ——, greatly surprised. “Who cares what the fellow said? You’re ill, Barton—definitely ill. Let me call a carriage.”

“Ill! No—not ill,” he said, clearly struggling to regain his composure. “But, to tell the truth, I’m tired—a little overworked, and perhaps too anxious. You know I’ve had a case in the Chancery court, and bringing a lawsuit to an end is always a nervous business. I’ve felt uncomfortable all evening, but I’m better now. Come, come—shall we go on?”
“No, no. Take my advice, Barton, and go home. You really do need rest! You look quite ill. I must insist that you let me see you home,” his friend replied.

I supported ——’s advice, all the more readily because Barton plainly did not mind being persuaded. He left us, declining our offer to accompany him. I did not know —— well enough to discuss the scene we had just witnessed. We exchanged only a few ordinary comments and expressions of concern. His manner, however, convinced me that he was as dissatisfied as I was with Barton’s hastily offered explanation of illness. We both suspected some hidden mystery behind that strange display.

The next day, I called at Barton’s lodgings to ask how he was. His servant told me that he had not left his room since returning the night before, but was not seriously ill and hoped to go out again in a few days. That evening he sent for Dr. R——, who then had a large and fashionable practice in Dublin. Their consultation is said to have been an odd one.

Barton described his symptoms in detail, but in a distracted, disconnected way that suggested a strange lack of interest in his own recovery. It was clear, at any rate, that something more important than his present illness was occupying his mind. He complained of occasional heart palpitations and headaches.

Among other questions, Doctor R—— asked whether anything irritating or worrying was occupying his thoughts. Barton denied it quickly and almost irritably. The doctor then gave his opinion: nothing was wrong beyond a slight digestive upset. He wrote a prescription and was about to leave when Barton called him back, with the air of a man remembering something he had nearly forgotten.

“Forgive me, Doctor, but I really did almost forget. May I ask you two or three medical questions? They may be rather odd, but a bet depends on the answers. I hope you’ll excuse such an unreasonable request.”
The doctor readily agreed to answer his questions.
Barton seemed to find it difficult to begin. He was silent for a minute, then walked to his bookcase and returned just as he had gone. At last he sat down and said—

“You’ll think these very childish questions, but I can’t collect my bet without a definite answer, so I must ask them. First, I want to know about lockjaw. Suppose a man really has had it and seems to have died of it—so convincingly that a doctor of average ability declares him actually dead. Could he recover after all?”
The doctor smiled and shook his head.

“But—but a mistake could be made,” Barton continued. “Suppose someone ignorant, pretending to have medical knowledge. Could some stage of the illness deceive him into mistaking an ordinary part of its progress for death itself?”
“No one who has ever seen death,” he answered, “could make that mistake in a case of lockjaw.”

Barton thought for a few minutes. “My next question may be even more childish. But first, tell me: are foreign hospitals—say, for example, one in Naples—run with very lax rules and little competence? Couldn’t all kinds of mistakes and slips occur when names and other details are entered in their records?”
Doctor R—— admitted that he did not know enough to answer that question.

“Well then, Doctor, here is my last question. You will probably laugh, but I must ask it all the same. Is there any disease among all human illnesses that could noticeably reduce a man’s height and entire frame? Could it make him shrink in every proportion, yet leave him looking exactly like himself in every detail, except for his height and size? Any disease, mind you—however rare, however little belief there may generally be in it—that could possibly produce such an effect?”
The doctor answered with a smile and a very firm no.
“Then tell me,” Barton said abruptly, “if a man has reasonable grounds to fear an attack from a madman who is still at large, can’t he obtain a warrant to have him arrested and detained?”
“That’s really a question for a lawyer, rather than someone in my profession,” replied Dr. R——. “But I believe a magistrate would order that if you applied to him.”

The doctor then said goodbye. Just as he reached the front door, however, he remembered leaving his cane upstairs and went back. His return was awkward. A piece of paper he recognised as his prescription was slowly burning in the fire. Barton sat close beside it, his face fixed in an expression of gloom and dismay.
Doctor R—— was too tactful to comment on what he saw. But he had seen enough to convince him that Captain Barton’s real suffering lay in his mind, not his body.
A few days later, the following advertisement appeared in the Dublin newspapers.

“If Sylvester Yelland, formerly a common sailor aboard His Majesty’s frigate Dolphin, or his nearest relatives will contact Mr. Hubert Smith, attorney, at his office in Dame Street, they may learn something greatly to their advantage. Those wishing to avoid being seen may call at any hour up to midnight. The strictest secrecy will be honourably maintained regarding every communication intended to be confidential.”

As I have mentioned, the Dolphin was the ship Captain Barton had commanded. Extraordinary efforts were made to give this strange notice the widest possible publicity, through handbills and other means as well as repeated advertisements. Taken together, these circumstances suggested to Dr. R—— that Barton’s extreme uneasiness was somehow connected with the person named in the notice, and that Barton himself was its author.
Needless to say, however, this was only a guess. The agent disclosed no information whatever about the advertisement’s real purpose, nor any hint of who had employed him.
CHAPTER IV.
HE TALKS WITH A CLERGYMAN.

Mr. Barton had lately begun to acquire a reputation as a morbidly anxious man, but he was still very far from deserving it. Although he was by no means lively, his moods were naturally steady and even. He was not prone to excessive low spirits.

He therefore soon began returning to his old habits. One of the earliest signs of this healthier state of mind was his appearance at a grand dinner of the Freemasons, a worthy brotherhood to which he himself belonged. At first Barton was gloomy and distracted. He drank much more freely than usual—possibly to drive away his secret anxieties. Under the influence of good wine and pleasant company, he gradually became talkative, and even noisy, which was quite unlike him.

He was still in these unusually high spirits when he left the company at about half past ten. And since a cheerful evening of drinking strongly encourages romantic attentions, it occurred to him to go straight to Lady L——’s and spend the rest of the evening with her and his bride-to-be.

He was soon in —— Street, chatting cheerfully with the ladies. It must not be supposed that Captain Barton had drunk more than good manners allowed on a social occasion. He had merely had enough wine to lift his spirits, without in the slightest degree unsettling his mind or affecting his manners.

With this unusually elevated mood, he had entirely forgotten—or dismissed with contempt—the vague fears that had weighed on his mind for so long and partly cut him off from society. But as the night passed and his artificial cheerfulness began to fade, those painful feelings gradually returned. He became as distracted and anxious as before.

At last he said goodnight, with an unpleasant sense that something bad was about to happen. His mind was haunted by a thousand mysterious fears. Even while he keenly felt their weight, he inwardly tried—or pretended—to despise them.
It was this proud defiance of what he considered his own weakness that now drove him to the course of action that brought about the encounter I am about to relate.
Mr. Barton could easily have called a coach. But he knew that his strong desire to do so came from nothing except what he desperately insisted, to himself, were his own superstitious fears.

He could also have gone home by a route other than the one his mysterious correspondent had warned him against. But for the same reason, he dismissed that idea too. With a stubborn, half-desperate determination, he resolved to force matters toward some kind of crisis, if there was anything real behind his earlier suffering. If there was not, he meant to prove to his own satisfaction that the whole thing was a delusion. He therefore chose to follow exactly the route he had taken on that painfully memorable night when his strange persecution began. Yet, in truth, no pilot steering his ship for the first time beneath the guns of an enemy battery ever had his resolve tested more severely. Captain Barton followed the lonely path, scarcely breathing. Despite every effort of reason and disbelief, he felt that it was haunted by some being hostile to him.

He walked steadily and quickly, scarcely breathing in the intensity of his suspense. But there was no return of the dreaded footsteps. He had safely covered more than three-quarters of the way and was beginning to feel his confidence return as he approached the long line of flickering oil lamps that marked the busy streets.

His feeling of self-congratulation lasted only a moment. The crack of a musket about a hundred yards behind him, and the whistle of a bullet close to his head, shattered it with a nasty shock. His first impulse was to go back and pursue the man who had tried to kill him. But, as we have said, the road was cluttered on either side by the foundations of an unfinished street. Beyond them lay empty fields full of rubbish and neglected lime and brick kilns. Everything was now utterly silent, as though no sound had ever disturbed that dark, ugly solitude. It was plainly useless to try to search alone for the would-be murderer in such surroundings. He could hear no retreating footsteps, or any other sound, to guide his pursuit.

Overwhelmed by the feelings of a man who has just escaped a murderous attack by the narrowest possible margin, Captain Barton turned away again. He hurried on his way, though he did not actually quicken his pace to a run.

As I have said, he had turned after pausing for a few seconds and had just begun his hurried retreat when he suddenly met the little man in the fur cap whom he remembered so well. The encounter lasted only a moment. The figure was walking at the same exaggerated speed, with the same strange air of menace as before. As it passed, he thought he heard it say in a furious whisper, “Still alive—still alive!”
The state of Mr. Barton’s mind was now beginning to produce a corresponding change in his health and appearance. The alteration became so great that it could not escape general notice and comment.

For reasons known only to himself, he took no steps whatever to report the attempt on his life, which he had so narrowly escaped, to the authorities. On the contrary, he guarded the secret closely. He did not mention it until many weeks afterward, and then only in strict confidence to a gentleman whom his mental torments finally compelled him to consult.

Despite his low spirits, however, poor Barton had no satisfactory explanation to give the world for neglecting the attentions his engagement to Miss Montague required. He was therefore obliged to make an effort and show a confident, cheerful face in public.

He guarded the true source of his suffering, and every circumstance connected with it, so fiercely that his secrecy raised at least a suspicion that he knew the cause of this strange persecution. It seemed to be something that, for his own sake, he could not or dared not reveal.

His mind had thus turned inward, constantly occupied with a haunting anxiety that he dared not reveal or confide to another human being. It grew more agitated every day, and naturally more sensitive to a form of attack that worked through his nervous system. In this state, he was destined to endure increasingly frequent, stealthy visits from the apparition that had seemed, from the beginning, to hold such terrible power over his imagination.
It was about this time that Captain Barton called on the preacher Dr. ——, who was celebrated in those days and whom he knew slightly. An extraordinary conversation followed.
The clergyman was sitting in his college rooms, surrounded by books on his favorite subject and deep in the study of theology, when Barton was announced.

Barton’s manner was both embarrassed and agitated. This, together with his pale, haggard face, made the scholar uncomfortably aware that his visitor must recently have suffered terribly to account for so striking—almost shocking—a change.

They exchanged the usual polite greetings and a few ordinary remarks. Captain Barton plainly noticed the surprise his visit had caused, which Doctor —— could not entirely conceal. Breaking a brief pause, he said—

“This is a strange visit, Doctor ——. Perhaps I hardly know you well enough to justify it. Under ordinary circumstances I would not have ventured to disturb you. But I have not intruded out of idleness or impertinence. I’m sure you will not think so when I tell you how much I am suffering.”
Doctor —— interrupted him with the reassurances that good manners called for, and Barton continued—

“I have come to ask for your advice, and so to make a demand on your patience. When I say your patience, I could go further. I could say your humanity—your compassion. For I have suffered greatly, and I am suffering still.”
“My dear sir,” the clergyman replied, “it would give me the greatest satisfaction to comfort you in any distress of mind. But—you know——”

“I know what you’re going to say,” Barton quickly replied. “I’m an unbeliever, and therefore incapable of finding help in religion. But don’t take that for granted. At least you must not assume that, however unsettled my beliefs may be, I don’t take a deep—a very deep—interest in the subject. Recent circumstances have forced it on my attention in a way that has compelled me to reconsider the whole question. I believe I am approaching it with a more open mind and a greater willingness to learn than ever before.”
“Your doubts concern the evidence for divine revelation, I assume,” the clergyman suggested.
“Well—no—not entirely. In fact, I’m ashamed to say that I haven’t even thought through my objections well enough to explain them clearly. But—but there is one subject that interests me particularly.”
He paused again, and Doctor —— urged him to go on.

“The fact is,” Barton said, “however uncertain I may be about the truth of what we are taught to call revelation, I am deeply and horribly convinced of one thing. There is a spiritual world beyond this one—a system whose workings are usually, mercifully, hidden from us. That system can be, and sometimes is, partly and terribly revealed. I am sure—I know,” Barton continued, growing more agitated, “that there is a God—a dreadful God—and that punishment follows guilt in the most mysterious and overwhelming ways, through the most inexplicable and terrifying powers. There is a spiritual order—great God, how I have been convinced of it!—an order that is malicious, impossible to appease, and all-powerful. Under its persecution I am suffering, and have been suffering, the torments of the damned! Yes, sir—yes—the fires and madness of hell!”

As Barton spoke, his agitation became so violent that the clergyman was shocked, and even alarmed. His wild, excited rush of words, and above all the indefinable horror stamped on his face, contrasted with his usual cool, unemotional self-control in a way that was striking and deeply painful.
CHAPTER V.
MR. BARTON STATES HIS CASE.

“My dear sir,” Doctor —— said after a short pause, “I fear you have indeed been very unhappy. But I venture to predict that the depression troubling you will prove to have purely physical causes. With a change of air and a few strengthening medicines, your spirits will recover, and your mind will be as cheerful and calm as before. There was, after all, more truth than we are quite willing to admit in the ancient theories. They attributed the excessive dominance of one mental state to overactivity or sluggishness in one or another bodily organ. Believe me, a little attention to diet, exercise, and the other essentials of health, under competent guidance, will make you as much yourself again as you could wish.”

“Doctor ——,” Barton said with something like a shudder, “I cannot deceive myself with that hope. There is only one hope I can cling to: that some other spiritual power, stronger than the one tormenting me, may fight it and free me. If that cannot happen, I am lost—lost now and forever.”
“But, Mr. Barton, you must remember,” his companion urged, “that others have suffered as you have, and——”

“No, no, no,” he interrupted irritably. “No, sir, I am not a gullible man—far from a superstitious one. Perhaps I have been too much the opposite—too skeptical, too slow to believe. But unless I were a man whom no amount of evidence could convince, unless I dismissed the repeated, the constant evidence of my own senses, I am now—now at last—forced to believe. I cannot escape the conviction—the overwhelming certainty—that wherever I go, I am haunted and followed by—by a DEMON!”
There was an unnatural intensity of horror in Barton’s face as he spoke these words, his damp, deathlike features turned toward his companion.
“God help you, my poor friend,” said Dr. ——, deeply shocked. “God help you, for you are indeed suffering, whatever may have caused your suffering.”
“Yes, yes, God help me,” Barton echoed grimly. “But will he help me—will he help me?”
“Pray to him—pray with humility and trust,” the clergyman said.

“Pray, pray,” he echoed again. “I can’t pray. I could just as easily move a mountain by an effort of will. I don’t have enough belief to pray. There is something inside me that will not pray. You’re asking for impossibilities—literal impossibilities.”
“You will not find it impossible if you only try,” said Doctor ——.

“Try! I have tried, and the attempt only fills me with confusion, and sometimes terror. I have tried in vain, and worse than in vain. Whenever my mind approaches the thought of the Creator, the terrible, inexpressible idea of eternity and infinity crushes me and drives me mad. I draw back from the effort in fear. I tell you, Doctor ——, if I am to be saved, it must be by some other means. The idea of an eternal Creator is unbearable to me. My mind cannot endure it.”
“Tell me, then, my dear sir,” he urged. “Tell me how you would like me to help you, what you want to learn from me, what I can do or say to bring you relief.”

“Listen to me first,” Captain Barton replied in a subdued manner, trying to suppress his agitation. “Listen while I describe the circumstances of the persecution that has made my life almost unbearable. It has made me fear death and the world beyond the grave as much as I have come to hate being alive.”
Barton then related the circumstances I have already described in detail, and continued:

“This has now become a regular thing—something familiar. I don’t mean actually seeing him in the flesh. Thank God, that at least is not permitted every day. Thank God, I have mercifully been allowed intervals of rest from the indescribable horror of those visits, though never any sense of safety. But I am never, for a single instant, free of the knowledge that a malicious spirit is following and watching me wherever I go. I am pursued by blasphemies, cries of despair and appalling hatred. I hear those dreadful sounds called after me as I turn street corners. They come at night while I sit alone in my room. They haunt me everywhere, accusing me of hideous crimes and—great God!—threatening me with approaching vengeance and eternal misery. Hush! Do you hear that?” he cried with a horrible smile of triumph. “There, there, will that convince you?”
The clergyman felt a chill of horror pass over him. In the wail of a sudden gust of wind, he heard—or thought he heard—half-formed sounds of rage and mockery mingling with its moan.
“Well, what do you think of that?” Barton cried at last, drawing a long breath through his teeth.
“I heard the wind,” said Doctor ——. “What should I think of it? What is remarkable about it?”
“The prince of the powers of the air,” Barton muttered with a shudder.

“Now, now, my dear sir,” the scholar said, trying to reassure himself. For even in broad daylight, there was something unpleasantly contagious about the nervous agitation from which his visitor suffered so miserably. “You must not give in to these wild imaginings. You must resist these impulses of the imagination.”
“Yes, yes, ‘Resist the devil, and he will flee from you,’” Barton said in the same tone. “But how do I resist him? Yes, that’s it—that’s the difficulty. What—what am I to do? What can I do?”
“My dear sir, this is imagination,” said the man of books. “You are tormenting yourself.”

“No, no, sir—imagination has nothing to do with it,” Barton answered rather sternly. “Imagination! Was that what made you, as well as me, hear those voices of hell just now? Imagination, indeed! No, no.”

“But you have seen this person frequently,” the clergyman said. “Why haven’t you spoken to him or seized him? Isn’t it a little hasty, to say the least, to assume as you have that a supernatural power is involved? After all, everything might be easily explained if the proper steps were taken to investigate it.”

“There are circumstances connected with this—this appearance,” Barton said, “that there is no need to reveal, but that prove its horrible nature to me. I know the being that follows me is not human. I say I know it. I could prove it to your satisfaction.” He paused for a minute, then added, “As for speaking to it, I dare not. I could not. When I see it, I am powerless. I stand under death’s gaze, before the triumphant power and malice of hell. My strength, my powers of thought, my memory—all desert me. O God, sir, I fear you don’t know what you’re talking about. Mercy, mercy; heaven have pity on me!”
He rested his elbow on the table and passed his hand across his eyes as though to shut out some image of horror, muttering the last words he had spoken over and over again.

“Doctor ——,” he said, suddenly straightening and looking directly at the clergyman with pleading eyes, “I know you will do whatever can be done for me. You now know all the circumstances and the nature of my suffering. I tell you, I cannot help myself. I have no hope of escape. I am utterly helpless. I beg you, then, to consider my case carefully. If anything can be done for me through prayers offered on my behalf, through the pleas of good people, or through any help or influence whatsoever, I implore you—I appeal to you in the name of the Most High—let me benefit from that influence. Deliver me from this body of death. Fight for me, pity me. I know you will. You cannot refuse me this. It is the purpose and object of my visit. Send me away with some hope, however small, some faint hope that I may finally be freed. Then I will gather the strength to endure, from hour to hour, the hideous dream my existence has become.”

Doctor —— assured him that all he could do was pray earnestly for him, and that he would certainly do so. They parted with a hurried, sorrowful farewell. Barton hastened to the carriage waiting at the door, pulled down the blinds, and drove away. Doctor —— returned to his room to reflect at leisure on the strange interview that had just interrupted his studies.
CHAPTER VI.
SEEN AGAIN.

Captain Barton’s changed and eccentric habits could hardly escape notice and discussion for long. People offered various theories to explain them. Some blamed the pressure of secret financial difficulties. Others thought he was reluctant to honor an engagement into which they assumed he had rushed too quickly. Still others suspected the beginnings of mental illness. This last explanation was indeed the most plausible, as well as the most widely accepted, of the theories circulating in the gossip of the day.

Miss Montague had, of course, noticed the change from its very beginning, gradual though it had been at first. The closeness of their relationship, and the deep personal interest it gave her, provided both the opportunity and the motive to make successful use of the sharp, penetrating powers of observation characteristic of her sex.

His visits had eventually become very irregular, and his manner during them was distracted, strange, and agitated. After hinting at her anxiety and suspicions more than once, Lady L—— finally stated her concern plainly and pressed him for an explanation.

He gave his explanation. At first, its nature relieved the worst fears of the old lady and her niece. But the circumstances surrounding it plainly suggested truly dreadful consequences for the now wretched man who had made this strange declaration—for his spirits, and indeed for his sanity. After only a little reflection, their minds filled with distress and alarm.

At last the young lady’s father, General Montague, arrived. He had known Barton slightly ten or twelve years earlier. Knowing his wealth and connections, he was inclined to consider him an entirely suitable, indeed highly desirable, husband for his daughter. He laughed at the story of Barton’s supernatural visitors and lost no time in calling on his future son-in-law.
“My dear Barton,” he said cheerfully after a little conversation, “my sister tells me that low spirits are tormenting you in quite a new and original form.”
Barton’s expression changed, and he gave a deep sigh.
“Come, come, this really won’t do,” the General continued. “You look more like a man on his way to the gallows than to the altar. These devils have made quite a saint of you.”
Barton tried to change the subject.

“No, no, that won’t do,” his visitor said, laughing. “I’m determined to say my piece about this magnificent make-believe mystery of yours. You mustn’t be angry, but really, it is too bad to see a man of your age frightened into good behavior like a naughty child threatened with a bogeyman—and, from all I hear, a very contemptible bogeyman at that. Seriously, what they tell me has annoyed me a good deal. But I’m also thoroughly convinced that there is nothing here that a little care and proper handling couldn’t clear up within a week at most.”
“Ah, General, you don’t know—” he began.

“Yes, but I know quite enough to justify my confidence,” the soldier interrupted. “Don’t I know that all your trouble comes from the occasional appearance of a certain little man in a cap and overcoat, with a red vest and an evil-looking face? He follows you about, pops up at the corners of lanes, and sends you into fits of shivering. Now, my dear fellow, I’ll make it my business to catch this mischievous little fraud. Before a month is out, I’ll either beat him to a jelly with my own hands or have him whipped through town at the back of a cart.”

“If you knew what I know,” Barton said with gloomy agitation, “you would speak very differently. Don’t imagine I’m so weak as to reach the conclusion I’ve been forced to accept without the most overwhelming proof. The proof is here, locked up here.” As he spoke, he tapped his chest. Then, with an anxious sigh, he continued pacing up and down the room.
“Well, well, Barton,” his visitor said, “I’ll bet a rump-steak dinner and a dozen bottles of wine that I’ll grab the ghost and convince even you before many days are out.”

He was continuing in the same vein when something suddenly stopped him and gave him a considerable shock. Barton had approached the window and was now staggering slowly backward like a man who had received a stunning blow. His arm was stretched toward the street. His face, and even his lips, were white as ashes, while he muttered, “There—by heaven!—there—there!”

General Montague automatically sprang to his feet. From the sitting-room window he saw a figure that, as far as he could judge in his haste, matched the description of the person whose appearances so persistently disturbed his friend’s peace.

The figure was just turning away from the railings around the basement area, where it had been leaning. Without waiting to see more, the old gentleman snatched up his cane and hat and rushed downstairs into the street, furiously hoping to seize the mysterious stranger and punish his insolence.

He looked around in vain for any trace of the person he himself had distinctly seen. He ran breathlessly to the nearest corner, expecting to catch sight of the retreating figure from there. But no such figure was visible. Back and forth he ran, from crossing to crossing, without finding a trace. Only when the curious stares and laughing faces of passersby reminded him how ridiculous his pursuit looked did he slow down. He lowered the walking cane he had unconsciously raised in a threatening position, adjusted his hat, and walked calmly back, though inwardly annoyed and flustered. He found Barton pale and shaking in every limb. Both remained silent, though their feelings were very different. At last Barton whispered, “You saw it?”

“It!—him—someone—you mean—of course I did,” Montague replied irritably. “But what good or harm is there in seeing him? The fellow runs as fast as a street lamplighter. I wanted to catch him, but he had slipped away before I could reach the front door. Still, it’s no great matter. Next time, I dare say, I’ll do better. And by God, if I ever get within reach of him, I’ll let his shoulders feel the weight of my cane.”

Despite General Montague’s promises and urging, however, Barton continued to suffer from the same unexplained cause. No matter how, when, or where he went, he was still constantly followed or confronted by the being that had gained such a horrible influence over him.
Nowhere, and at no time, was he safe from the repulsive figure that haunted him with such devilish persistence.

His depression, misery, and agitation became more deeply rooted and alarming every day. The mental agonies that preyed on him without pause finally began to affect his health so noticeably that Lady L—— and General Montague persuaded him, without much difficulty, to try a short tour of continental Europe. They hoped that a complete change of scene would at least break the influence of familiar associations. His more skeptical friends believed that these associations played a real part in suggesting and sustaining what they considered merely a form of nervous delusion.

General Montague, however, was convinced that the figure haunting his future son-in-law was certainly not a creation of his imagination. On the contrary, he believed it was a solid being of flesh and blood, determined to watch and follow the unfortunate gentleman—perhaps with some murderous purpose in view.

Even that explanation was not a very pleasant one. Yet it was clear that if Barton could ever be convinced there was nothing supernatural in what he had so far considered supernatural, the affair would lose all its terror for him. It would entirely cease to have the harmful effect on his health and spirits that it had had until now. The General therefore reasoned that if Barton actually escaped the harassment simply by traveling and changing his surroundings, it plainly could not have come from any supernatural power.
CHAPTER VII.
FLIGHT.

Giving in to their persuasion, Barton left Dublin for England with General Montague. They travelled quickly by carriage to London, then on to Dover, where they took the passenger boat to Calais with a favourable wind. Since leaving the shores of Ireland, the General had grown more confident each day that the journey would improve Barton's spirits. To Barton's indescribable relief and delight, he had not once since then even imagined a return of those impressions that had gradually dragged him into the depths of despair at home.

This release from what he had begun to regard as the inevitable condition of his life, and the sense of safety beginning to spread through his mind, brought him happiness beyond words. Exulting in what he believed was his deliverance, he imagined a thousand happy possibilities for a future he had so recently scarcely dared to consider. In short, both he and his companion privately congratulated themselves on the end of the persecution that had caused its direct victim such unspeakable agony.

It was a beautiful day, and a crowd of idle onlookers stood on the jetty to meet the passenger boat and enjoy the bustle of the new arrivals. Montague walked a few steps ahead of his friend. As he made his way through the crowd, a little man touched his arm and said in a strong regional dialect—
“You are walking too fast, sir. You will lose your sick companion in the crowd, for, by my faith, the poor gentleman seems to be fainting.”
Montague turned quickly and saw that Barton did indeed look deathly pale. He hurried to his side.
“My dear fellow, are you ill?” he asked anxiously.
The question went unanswered. He repeated it twice before Barton stammered—
“I saw him—by——, I saw him!”
“Him! The wretch—who—where now? Where is he?” cried Montague, looking around.
“I saw him—but he is gone,” Barton repeated faintly.
“But where—where? For God's sake, speak,” Montague urged with desperate intensity.
“Just a moment ago—here,” he said.
“But what did he look like? What did he have on? What was he wearing? Quickly, quickly!” urged his excited companion, ready to dart into the crowd and seize the offender on the spot.
“He touched your arm—he spoke to you—he pointed to me. God be merciful to me, there is no escape,” Barton said in the low, subdued tones of despair.

Montague had already rushed off in a flurry of mingled hope and rage. But although the distinctive appearance of the stranger who had spoken to him was vividly fixed in his memory, he could find no one in the crowd who bore even the slightest resemblance to him.
He enlisted several bystanders in the fruitless search. Believing he had been robbed, they helped all the more eagerly. At last, out of breath and baffled, he abandoned the attempt.

“Ah, my friend, it will do no good,” said Barton. His voice was faint, and he had the bewildered, ghastly look of someone stunned by a mortal shock. “There is no use in struggling. Whatever it is, the dreadful bond between me and it is now established. I shall never escape—never!”

“Nonsense, nonsense, my dear Barton. Don't talk like that,” said Montague, with both irritation and dismay. “You must not, I tell you. We shall outwit the scoundrel yet. Never mind, I say—never mind.”
From then on, however, any attempt to give Barton even a ray of hope was wasted effort. He sank into despair.

This intangible influence, seemingly far too slight to have such an effect, was rapidly wearing away his mental powers, his strength of character, and his health. His first concern now was to return to Ireland, where he believed, and now almost hoped, he would soon die.

He returned to Ireland accordingly, and one of the first faces he saw on the shore was once again that of his relentless and dreaded follower. Barton seemed at last to have lost not only all enjoyment and every hope in life, but all independence of will as well. He now submitted passively to the care and direction of the friends most concerned for his welfare.

With the apathy of complete despair, he agreed without question to whatever measures they suggested and advised. As a last resort, they decided to move him to a house belonging to Lady L—— near Clontarf. His doctor still insisted that this entire sequence of effects arose merely from some disorder of the nerves. On his advice, they resolved that Barton should remain strictly indoors and use only those rooms overlooking an enclosed yard, whose gates were to be kept securely locked.

These precautions would certainly protect him from the chance appearance of any living figure that his excited imagination might mistake for the spectre. It was argued that his imagination recognised this spectre in every figure bearing even a vague or general resemblance to the peculiar features it had first given the apparition.

They hoped that a month or six weeks of complete seclusion under these conditions would interrupt the series of terrible impressions. This might gradually dispel the fears that made him susceptible, along with the associations that had reinforced the supposed illness and made recovery hopeless.

He was to have constant cheerful company and the company of his friends. On the whole, they were very hopeful that the treatment just described would finally overcome the patient's stubborn state of morbid anxiety.

Lady L——, General Montague, and the General's daughter—Barton's own promised bride—therefore accompanied poor Barton. He himself never dared to hope that he would finally be freed from the horrors under which his life was literally wasting away. He now took possession of the rooms whose position protected him from the intrusions he dreaded with such unspeakable terror.

After a little while, their steady persistence in this system began to produce a very noticeable, though gradual, improvement in both the patient's health and his spirits. Nothing approaching a complete recovery could yet be seen. On the contrary, anyone who had not seen him since the beginning of his strange sufferings might well have been shocked by the change in him.

Still, such improvement as there was brought gratitude and delight, especially to the young lady. Her attachment to him, together with the particularly painful position in which his prolonged illness had placed her, made her scarcely less deserving of pity than Barton himself.

A week passed—a fortnight—a month—and still the hated visitation had not returned. So far, the treatment had been entirely successful. The chain of associations was broken. The constant pressure on his exhausted spirits had been lifted. Under these comparatively favourable circumstances, a sense of connection with the world around him, and something of human interest, if not enjoyment, began to bring him back to life.

About this time, Lady L——, who, like most older ladies of the day, was deeply versed in family remedies and laid great claim to medical knowledge, sent her own maid to the kitchen garden. She gave her a list of herbs to gather carefully and bring back to her housekeeper for the purpose she had specified. The maid returned, however, with her task scarcely half finished, and in considerable agitation and alarm. Her explanation for her hurried retreat and obvious distress was strange, and startled the old lady.
CHAPTER VIII.
SOFTENED.

It appeared that she had gone to the kitchen garden as her mistress had instructed, and begun choosing the specified plants from the overgrown, neglected herbs crowding one corner of the enclosure. While engaged in this pleasant work, she casually sang part of an old song, as she said, “to keep herself company.” An ill-natured laugh interrupted her. Looking up, she saw through the old thorn hedge surrounding the garden a remarkably ugly little man, whose face bore an expression of menace and malice. He stood close to her, on the other side of the hawthorn screen.

She said she had been completely unable to move or speak while he instructed her to deliver a message to Captain Barton. She distinctly remembered its substance: Captain Barton must go out as usual and let his friends see him outdoors, or else prepare for a visit in his own room.

After delivering this brief message, the stranger had climbed down into the ditch outside with a threatening air. Seizing the hawthorn stems in his hands, he seemed about to climb through the hedge, something he could have done without much difficulty.

Without waiting for that to happen, of course, the girl had dropped her treasures of thyme and rosemary, turned, and run to the house with the speed of terror. Lady L—— ordered her, on pain of immediate dismissal, to say absolutely nothing about any part of the incident that concerned Captain Barton. At the same time, she sent her men to search the garden and adjoining fields at once. As usual, the search was unsuccessful. Filled with misgivings she could not define, Lady L—— told her brother what had happened. The story went no further until long afterwards and was, of course, carefully kept from Barton, who continued to improve, though slowly.

Barton now began occasionally walking in the courtyard I have mentioned. A high wall enclosed it, blocking every view beyond its boundaries. He therefore felt perfectly safe there, and, if one of the stablehands had not carelessly broken the rules, he might have enjoyed his much-prized freedom from persecution for at least a little longer. The yard opened onto the public road through a wooden gate with a smaller door set into it, and an iron gate outside provided further protection. Strict orders had been given to keep both carefully locked. Despite these orders, one day Barton was slowly pacing the narrow enclosure on his usual walk. He had reached the far end and was turning to retrace his steps when he saw the small wooden door standing ajar, and his tormentor's face staring motionlessly at him through the iron bars. For a few seconds he stood rooted to the ground, breathless and drained of colour, held spellbound by that dreaded gaze. Then he collapsed unconscious and helpless onto the paving.

He was found there a few minutes later and carried to his room—the room he would never leave alive. From then on, a marked and inexplicable change could be seen in his state of mind. Captain Barton was no longer the agitated, despairing man he had been. A strange change had come over him. An unearthly calm ruled his mind: it was the stillness of the grave felt in advance.

“Montague, my friend, this struggle is almost over now,” he said calmly, but with a look of fixed and fearful awe. “At last I have received some comfort from that world of spirits from which my punishment came. I know now that my sufferings will soon be over.”
Montague urged him to go on.

“Yes,” he said in a softened voice, “my punishment is almost over. Perhaps I shall never escape sorrow, in this life or in eternity, but my agony is nearly finished. Comfort has been revealed to me, and I shall bear what remains of my allotted struggle with submission—even with hope.”
“I am glad to hear you speak so calmly, my dear Barton,” said Montague. “Peace and cheerfulness of mind are all you need to become your old self again.”
“No, no—I can never be that,” he said mournfully. “I am no longer fit for life. I shall soon die. I am to see him only once more, and then everything is over.”
“He told you so, then?” suggested Montague.

“He? No, no: good news could hardly come through him. And this news was good and welcome. It came so solemnly and sweetly, with unspeakable love and sadness. I could not fully explain it to you without saying more than is necessary or fitting about other scenes and people from long ago.” As Barton said this, he shed tears.

“Come, come,” said Montague, misunderstanding the source of his emotion. “You must not give way. After all, what is it but a pack of dreams and nonsense? Or, at worst, the tricks of some scheming scoundrel who enjoys his power to play on your nerves and loves to use it—a sneaking vagabond who holds a grudge against you and settles it this way because he does not dare try a more manly one.”

“He does indeed hold a grudge against me—you are right,” said Barton, with a sudden shudder. “A grudge, as you call it. Oh, my God! When Heaven's justice allows the Evil One to carry out a plan of revenge—when the task is entrusted to the lost and terrible victim of sin, whose own ruin was caused by the man, the very man, he is sent to pursue—then indeed the torments and terrors of hell are felt in advance on earth. But Heaven has treated me mercifully. Hope has opened to me at last. If death could come without the dreadful sight I am doomed to see, I would gladly close my eyes on the world this moment. But although death is welcome, I shrink with an agony you cannot understand—an actual frenzy of terror—from the last encounter with that—that demon who has drawn me to the edge of the chasm and who will himself plunge me down. I am to see him again—once more—but in circumstances unspeakably more terrifying than ever.”

As Barton spoke, he trembled so violently that Montague was truly alarmed by the intensity of his sudden agitation. He quickly tried to guide him back to the subject that had seemed to bring his mind such peace.
“It was not a dream,” he said after a time. “I was in a different state—I felt different and strange. Yet it was all as real, as clear and vivid, as what I see and hear now. It was a reality.”
“And what did you see and hear?” his companion urged.

“When I woke from the fainting spell I fell into when I saw him,” Barton said, continuing as though he had not heard the question, “it was slowly, very slowly. I was lying beside a broad lake, with misty hills all around, and a soft, melancholy, rose-coloured light illuminating everything. It was unusually sad and lonely, yet more beautiful than any earthly scene. My head rested in a girl's lap, and she was singing a song that told—I do not know how, whether through words or harmonies—of my whole life, all that was past and all that was still to come. With the song, the old feelings I thought had died within me returned, and tears flowed from my eyes. They came partly because of the song and its mysterious beauty, and partly because of the unearthly sweetness of her voice. And yet I knew the voice—oh, how well! I was spellbound as I listened and looked at the lonely scene, without moving, almost without breathing—and, alas, alas, without turning my eyes towards the face I knew was near me. So sweet and powerful was the enchantment that held me. Then, slowly, the song and the scene grew fainter and fainter to my senses, until everything was dark and still again. And then I woke to this world, as you saw, comforted, for I knew that much had been forgiven me.” Barton again wept long and bitterly.

From this time on, as we have said, his prevailing mood was one of deep and tranquil sadness. But it was not uninterrupted. He was utterly convinced that he would experience one more, final visitation, surpassing in horror everything he had already endured. He often recoiled from that expected but unknown agony in fits of abject terror and frantic distress that filled the whole household with dismay and superstitious panic. Even those who claimed not to believe in supernatural involvement were often secretly troubled, in the silence of the night, by fears and misgivings they would not readily have admitted. None tried to persuade Barton to abandon his decision, which he now consistently followed, to shut himself in his room. Its window blinds were kept strictly down. His own servant was seldom away from him, day or night, and slept in a bed in the same room.

This man was a devoted and respectable servant. In addition to a valet's usual duties, which Barton's habit of doing things for himself generally made unnecessary, he had to attend carefully to the simple precautions by which his master hoped to keep out the dreaded intrusion of the “Watcher.” These arrangements amounted merely to making sure that no uncovered window or open door could expose his master to the dreaded influence. Besides attending to them, the valet was never to leave him alone. Complete solitude, even for a minute, had now become almost as unbearable to Barton as the thought of going out into the public streets. It was an instinctive anticipation of what was coming.
CHAPTER IX.
MAY HE REST.

Under these circumstances, of course, no steps were taken towards fulfilling his engagement to be married. The difference in age, and indeed in habits, between the young lady and Captain Barton had been quite enough to prevent her from forming any very passionate or romantic attachment to him. Although distressed and anxious, therefore, she was far from heartbroken.

Miss Montague nevertheless devoted much of her time to patient but fruitless attempts to cheer the unhappy invalid. She read to him and talked with him. But it was clear that, however hard he tried, every effort to escape the one ever-wakeful fear that preyed on him was utterly and miserably useless.

Young ladies are very fond of keeping pets. Among those who enjoyed Miss Montague's favour was a fine old owl that the gardener had caught sleeping in the ivy of a ruined stable and dutifully presented to her.

The whim that governs such preferences showed itself in the extravagant favour this grim, ugly bird immediately received from his mistress. Trivial as this odd circumstance may seem, I must mention it because, strangely enough, it is connected with the story's final scene.

Far from sharing this fondness for the new favourite, Barton regarded it from the beginning with an aversion as violent as it was utterly inexplicable. He could not bear even to be near it. His hatred and dread seemed so intense as to be laughable. To anyone who has never witnessed such an aversion, it would seem almost incredible.

With these few words of preliminary explanation, I shall give the details of the last scene in this strange series of events. It was nearly two o'clock one winter night, and Barton was in bed, as usual at that hour. The servant we have mentioned occupied a smaller bed in the same room, and a light was burning. His master suddenly woke him and said—

“I can't get it out of my head that that accursed bird has somehow got out and is lurking in a corner of the room. I have been dreaming about him. Get up, Smith, and look around. Search for him. Such hateful dreams!”

The servant got up and searched the room. As he did so, he heard the familiar sound, more like a long, drawn-out gasp than a hiss, with which these birds, from their hidden roosts, fill the quiet of the night with alarm.

This ghostly sign of its nearness guided the servant's search: the sound came from the passage onto which Barton's bedroom door opened. He opened the door and went a step or two forward to drive the bird away. He had scarcely entered the lobby, however, when the door slowly swung shut behind him, apparently moved by a gentle current of air. Directly above the door was a kind of window, intended to help light the passage during the day. The candlelight now shone through it, allowing the valet to see quite enough for his purpose.

As he went forward, he heard his master call him by name and tell him to place the candle on the table beside his bed. Lying in a bed well screened by curtains, Barton apparently had not noticed him leave the room. The servant was now some distance down the long passage. He did not want to raise his voice to answer, for fear of startling the sleeping household, and began hurrying softly back. Then, to his amazement, he heard a voice inside the bedroom answer calmly. Through the window above the door, he actually saw the light slowly moving, as though someone was carrying it across the room in response to his master's call. Paralysed by something like terror, though mixed with curiosity, he stood breathless and listening at the threshold, unable to find the courage to push open the door and go in. Then came a rustling of curtains and a sound like someone quietly soothing a child to sleep. In the midst of it, he heard Barton say in a tone of stifled horror, “Oh, God—oh, my God!” and repeat the same cry several times. Silence followed, then the same strange soothing sound broke it again. At last, in one swelling burst, came a yell of agony so appalling and hideous that an impulse of uncontrollable horror drove the man to the door. He tried with all his strength to force it open. Whether in his agitation he had failed to turn the handle fully, or whether the door really was secured from inside, he could not get in. As he pulled and pushed, yell after yell rang louder and wilder through the room, accompanied all the while by the same hushed sounds. Freezing with terror and scarcely knowing what he did, the man turned and ran down the passage, wringing his hands in extreme horror and indecision. At the head of the stairs he met General Montague, frightened and full of urgency. Just as they met, the fearful sounds stopped.
“What is it? Who—where is your master?” said Montague, incoherent with extreme agitation. “Has anything—for God's sake, is anything wrong?”
“Lord have mercy on us, it's all over,” said the man, staring wildly towards his master's bedroom. “He's dead, sir, I'm sure he's dead.”

Without waiting for questions or explanations, Montague hurried to the bedroom door, closely followed by the servant. He turned the handle and pushed it open. As the door gave way under his hand, the ill-omened bird the servant had been looking for suddenly sprang from the far side of the bed, uttering its ghostly warning. It flew through the doorway close above their heads, putting out the candle Montague carried as it passed. Then it crashed through the skylight above the lobby and sailed away into the darkness outside.
“There it is, God bless us,” the man whispered after a breathless pause.
“Curse that bird,” muttered the General, startled by its sudden appearance and unable to hide how shaken he was.
“The candle has been moved,” said the man after another breathless pause, pointing to the candle still burning in the room. “Look, they put it beside the bed.”
“Open the curtains, man, and don't stand there gaping,” Montague whispered sternly.
The man hesitated.

“Hold this, then,” said Montague, impatiently thrusting the candlestick into the servant's hand. He went to the bedside himself and drew the curtains apart. The candle still burning beside the bed lit a figure huddled together and half upright at its head. It looked as though it had shrunk back as far as the solid panelling would allow, and its hands were still clutching the bedclothes.

“Barton, Barton, Barton!” cried the General, with a strange mixture of awe and urgency. He took the candle and held it so that it shone directly on the face. The features were fixed, stern, and white. The jaw hung open, and the sightless eyes, still open, stared blankly ahead towards the front of the bed. “God Almighty! He's dead,” muttered the General, looking at this fearful sight. They both continued to stare at it in silence for a minute or more. “And cold, too,” Montague whispered, taking his hand away from the dead man's.
“And look, look—may I never draw another breath, sir,” the man added after another pause, shuddering, “if there wasn't something else on the bed with him. Look there—look there—see that, sir.”
As he spoke, the man pointed to a deep indentation near the foot of the bed, as though something heavy had pressed on it.
Montague said nothing.
“Come, sir, come away, for God's sake,” the man whispered. He drew close and held tightly to Montague's arm, glancing fearfully around. “What good can be done here now? Come away, for God's sake!”

At that moment they heard the footsteps of more than one person approaching. Montague hastily told the servant to stop them from coming any further. He then tried to release the dead man's rigid fingers from their grip on the bedclothes and, as well as he could, eased the dreadful figure back into a reclining position. Carefully closing the curtains around it, he hurried out himself to meet the approaching people.

There is no need to follow the later lives of those people so slightly connected with this account. It is enough to say that no clue was ever found to explain these mysterious events. So long a time has now passed since the event I have just described brought this strange history to an end that we can scarcely expect time to throw any new light on its dark and inexplicable outline. Until the secrets of the earth are no longer hidden, these events must therefore remain wrapped in their original mystery.

Only one event in Captain Barton's earlier life was ever mentioned as having a possible connection with the sufferings that ended his existence—sufferings he himself seemed to regard as punishment for some grave sin in his past. This event did not come to light until several years after his death. The disclosure was painful to his relatives and damaging to his memory.

It appeared that about six years before Captain Barton's final return to Dublin, he had formed an illicit relationship in the town of Plymouth. It was with the daughter of a member of the ship's crew under his command. Her father had punished his unhappy daughter's failing with extreme harshness and even brutality, and it was said that she had died of a broken heart. Taking advantage of Barton's share in her guilt, the man had treated him with marked insolence. Barton retaliated for this, and for what he resented with still more bitter anger—the man's treatment of the unfortunate girl—by systematically using the terrible, arbitrary punishments that naval regulations placed at the disposal of those responsible for discipline. Eventually the man escaped while the ship was in port at Naples. But he died, it was said, in a hospital in that town, from the wounds inflicted during one of his recent bloody punishments.

It is, of course, impossible to say whether these circumstances really have any connection with the events of Barton's later life. It seems more than likely, however, that in his own mind, at least, they were closely linked. But whatever the truth about the origin and motives of this mysterious persecution, there can be no doubt that a complete and impenetrable mystery about the forces through which it was carried out is likely to remain until Judgment Day.
POSTSCRIPT BY THE EDITOR.

The preceding account is given in the exact words of the good old clergyman, who supplied it to Doctor Hesselius in his own handwriting. Despite the occasional stiffness and repetition of his sentences, I thought it better to preserve my ability to assure the reader that, in handing the manuscript of so extraordinary an account to the printer, the Editor has not changed one letter of the original text.—[Editor, Papers of Dr. Hesselius.]
